summary.text: A metabolic pathway is a linked series of chemical reactions inside a cell, where the product of one enzyme usually becomes the substrate for the next.
Anabolic pathways build molecules using energy, while catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy that the building pathways then use.
How much flows through a pathway is regulated by the needs of the cell and the availability of the substrate, which helps maintain homeostasis.

facts.label: Two main types
facts.value: Anabolic (builds with energy) and catabolic (breaks down)

facts.label: Amphibolic pathway
facts.value: Can be catabolic or anabolic, depending on energy need or availability

facts.label: Location matters
facts.value: Different pathways run in different parts of a eukaryotic cell

facts.label: Cycles
facts.value: Some pathways loop, as the Krebs cycle does

items.prompt: A cell builds a large, complex molecule out of smaller pieces. Where does the energy for that job come from?

options.label: From the building reactions themselves, which give off energy
From catabolic pathways, whose breakdown reactions provide it
From waste side products that the cell recycles at the end
From enzymes, which hand over energy when they bind

items.explain: The breakdown in a catabolic pathway provides the energy that an anabolic pathway uses for biosynthesis.

items.prompt: Enzyme one in a pathway makes a molecule. What usually happens to that molecule next?

options.label: It is removed from the cell as waste straight away
It is held back until the whole pathway has finished
It switches off the enzyme that made it every time
It serves as the substrate for the next enzyme in the pathway

items.explain: In most pathways the product of one enzyme is the substrate of the next, and only side products are treated as waste.

items.prompt: A cell's demand for a product rises and falls through the day. What changes in the pathway making it?

options.label: How much flows through it, set by cell needs and substrate supply
Its enzymes swap places so the pathway runs in a new order
The pathway splits into two copies, one for each shift
Nothing, because pathways always run at one fixed rate

items.explain: The flux of metabolites through a pathway is regulated depending on the needs of the cell and the availability of the substrate.

items.prompt: A cell has one pathway that makes a particular amino acid. How is that amino acid typically broken down?

options.label: By the same pathway running backward
By the same enzymes in reverse order
By a separate and distinct pathway
It cannot be broken down inside the cell

items.explain: Pathways are often considered to flow in one direction, so synthesis and breakdown of an amino acid usually use separate pathways.

items.prompt: Building and breaking down molecules can happen in the same eukaryotic cell. How are the two kept from getting in each other's way?

options.label: They run only at different hours of the day
They share every enzyme but use opposite temperatures
Each uses enzymes borrowed from neighbouring cells
Separate organelles, or different enzymes and co-factors

items.explain: Anabolic and catabolic pathways in eukaryotes are separated physically by compartments or biochemically by needing different enzymes and co-factors.

items.prompt: A eukaryotic cell is running fatty acid biosynthesis and the electron transport chain. How do their locations compare?

options.label: Both take place in the mitochondrial membrane
Biosynthesis is in the cytosol; the chain is in the mitochondrial membrane
Both take place in the cytosol of the cell
The chain is in the cytosol; biosynthesis is in the mitochondrial membrane

items.explain: Fatty acid biosynthesis occurs in the cytosol, while the electron transport chain takes place in the mitochondrial membrane.

pack.title: Reactions that pass the baton
pack.question: How does a cell turn one molecule into another through a chain of reactions?

beats.title: Reactions that pass the baton
beats.hook: Cells rarely do a big job in one move; they hand a product from one enzyme to the next.

beats.prompt: Building a protein is unfavourable on its own, because it needs energy. What lets the cell go ahead anyway?
beats.explain: Anabolism has a positive Gibbs free energy (+ΔG) by itself, so it is coupled with an exergonic reaction that supplies the energy.

choices.label: The protein builds itself once enough enzymes are nearby
choices.feedback: Enzymes speed reactions, but an unfavourable reaction still needs an energy input.

choices.label: The cell waits for the reaction to turn spontaneous
choices.feedback: On its own the reaction stays non-spontaneous, so waiting does not help.

choices.label: It is coupled to an energy-releasing reaction

beats.prompt: Match each type of pathway to what it does.

right.label: Breaks molecules down and releases energy
Either one, depending on energy need or availability

beats.explain: Anabolic and catabolic pathways complement each other, and an amphibolic pathway can act as either.

beats.prompt: Where in a eukaryotic cell does each process take place?
beats.explain: Glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and fatty acid biosynthesis occur in the cytosol, while the chain and oxidative phosphorylation use the mitochondrial membrane.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: All chemical reactions are technically reversible.
In a cell, conditions often favour flux in one direction of a reaction.
So a cell breaks down an amino acid by running its building pathway backward.
That is why pathways are often considered to flow in one direction.

beats.explain: The breakdown of an amino acid may occur via a separate and distinct pathway from the one that makes it.

beats.idea: In a metabolic pathway, each reaction's product feeds the next, and anabolic and catabolic pathways trade energy.

paragraphs.heading: A chain of reactions
paragraphs.text: A metabolic pathway is a chain of chemical reactions that happen one after another inside a cell. The molecules involved, whether starting materials, in-between forms or end products, are called metabolites. Enzymes drive each step, and usually what one enzyme makes becomes the starting material, or substrate, of the next. Side products are treated as waste and removed from the cell.

paragraphs.heading: Building up and breaking down
paragraphs.text: Pathways come in two main kinds. Anabolic pathways spend energy to build molecules, joining smaller ones into larger, more complex ones. Catabolic pathways break complex molecules apart and release energy as they go. The two fit together, because the energy freed by breaking down pays for the building up. A third kind, the amphibolic pathway, can work either way, depending on how much energy is needed or available.

paragraphs.heading: Paying for the work
paragraphs.text: Catabolic pathways store the energy they release in carrier molecules. They add a high-energy phosphate bond to ADP and GDP, making ATP and GTP, and they also make carriers such as NADH and NADPH from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Their end products are often carbon dioxide, water and ammonia. Anabolic pathways, which build things like proteins, nucleic acids and lipids, are unfavorable on their own, because their reactions have a positive Gibbs free energy (+ΔG). They need to be coupled to an exergonic reaction that supplies chemical energy.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly one-way streets
paragraphs.text: Pathways are usually thought of as running in one direction. Every chemical reaction can in principle go backwards, but conditions in the cell often make one direction more favorable. So a cell may build an amino acid by one pathway and break it down by a separate one. Some steps are locked: as glucose enters a cell, ATP at once adds a phosphate to it, making glucose 6-phosphate in an irreversible first step.

paragraphs.heading: Glucose, the exception
paragraphs.text: Glucose handling bends this rule. Glycolysis breaks glucose down, yet several of its reactions can reverse and help rebuild glucose, a process called gluconeogenesis. This happens in the liver, and sometimes in the kidney, to keep blood glucose at the right level and supply the brain and muscles. It is not a perfect mirror of glycolysis: four of its enzymes are different, and they let it proceed spontaneously. When fats or proteins are plentiful, parts of glycolysis can also run backward to make glucose 6-phosphate for storage as glycogen or starch.

paragraphs.heading: Shared by all life
paragraphs.text: A core set of energy-producing catabolic pathways is found, in some form, in every living thing. All cells can carry out anaerobic respiration through glycolysis. Most organisms can also use the more efficient aerobic respiration of the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria go further, using sunlight to build compounds from non-living matter by photosynthesis.
